intent.raw_query: Iceland Northern Lights and hot springs, $3500 couple, January

experiences.name: Northern Lights Hunting Tour
experiences.description: Join a guided evening tour away from Reykjavik's light pollution to witness the aurora borealis dancing across the sky. Expert guides use real-time forecasts to find the best viewing spots, and you'll learn about the science behind this natural phenomenon while capturing stunning photographs.

experiences.name: Blue Lagoon Geothermal Spa
experiences.description: Soak in the world-famous milky-blue geothermal waters rich in silica and minerals. Enjoy in-water massages, silica mud masks, and swim-up bars while surrounded by dramatic lava fields. Book the Comfort package for access to the main lagoon, towel rental, and one silica mud mask.

experiences.name: Snorkeling or Diving in Silfra Fissure
experiences.description: Snorkel or dive between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates in crystal-clear glacial water with visibility up to 100 meters. The surreal blue and green hues of the water make this one of the most unique natural experiences on Earth, guided by certified instructors.

experiences.name: Secret Lagoon Natural Hot Spring
experiences.description: Relax in Iceland's oldest swimming pool, a naturally heated geothermal pool surrounded by bubbling hot springs and a small geyser that erupts every few minutes. Far less crowded than the Blue Lagoon, this authentic experience offers a peaceful soak amid stunning Icelandic countryside.

experiences.name: Skaftafell Glacier Hike on Vatnajökull
experiences.description: Strap on crampons and hike across Europe's largest glacier with an expert guide. Explore stunning ice formations, deep blue crevasses, and ash layers from ancient volcanic eruptions. The hike offers breathtaking panoramic views of the surrounding black sand plains and mountain peaks.

trip_options.title: Budget Explorer - Iceland
trip_options.description: Save money without sacrificing the experience. Perfect for travelers who value authentic local experiences over luxury.

day_by_day.morning: Arrive at Keflavik International Airport at 06:10. Clear customs and collect luggage. Take the Flybus or a budget shuttle to Reykjavik BSI terminal, then arrange onward travel north toward Siglufjörður. The drive is approximately 4-5 hours via Route 1 and the Héðinsfjörður tunnel. Rest and recover from the flight during the journey.
day_by_day.afternoon: Arrive in Siglufjörður in the early afternoon. Check in early if possible at Hotel Siglunes on Lækjargata 10, or store luggage and take a gentle walk along the harbour front to get oriented. Siglufjörður is a charming small fishing town nestled in a dramatic fjord — explore the colourful wooden houses and the quiet harbour area.
day_by_day.evening: Settle into the hotel and rest after the long travel day. As darkness falls (which comes early in January), step outside or find a dark spot near the harbour to watch for the Northern Lights — January is prime aurora season in Iceland. Dress in all your warmest layers.

meals.breakfast: Grab a snack or coffee at Keflavik Airport before departure — budget around 1,500–2,000 ISK for a pastry and coffee.
meals.lunch: Pack sandwiches or snacks from a Reykjavik Bonus or Krónan supermarket during your transit stop to save money on the road.
meals.dinner: Kaffi Rauðka in Siglufjörður — a cosy local café and restaurant offering hearty Icelandic soups and fish dishes. Budget around 2,500–3,500 ISK for a main course.

day_by_day.notes: January days in Siglufjörður are very short — expect only about 4–5 hours of daylight. The Héðinsfjörður tunnel (opened 2010) connects Siglufjörður to Ólafsfjörður and makes access much easier. Check road conditions on road.is before driving as mountain roads can be icy or closed in January.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the Herring Era Museum (Síldarminjasafnið) — one of Iceland's most celebrated regional museums, winner of the Council of Europe Museum Prize. It tells the fascinating story of the herring boom that made Siglufjörður prosperous. Entry is around 2,200 ISK. Note: confirm winter opening hours in advance as they may be limited.
day_by_day.afternoon: Walk the Siglufjörður town trail — a self-guided loop around the town taking in the old fish factory ruins, the church, and the scenic fjord views. The surrounding mountains are dramatic even in winter. If conditions allow, hike a short distance up the hillside above town for panoramic views of the fjord below.
day_by_day.evening: Northern Lights hunt from the hillside above Siglufjörður or along the fjord road away from town lights. The low light pollution in this remote area makes it excellent for aurora viewing. Check the Icelandic Met Office aurora forecast at en.vedur.is before heading out.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered at the hotel — pick up bread, skyr, eggs and fruit from the local Samkaup-Strax convenience store in Siglufjörður.
meals.lunch: Packed lunch from supermarket supplies — skyr, rye bread with smoked salmon or cheese, and fruit. Eat at the museum café if open.
meals.dinner: Cook a simple meal in the hotel if kitchen facilities are available, or return to Kaffi Rauðka for their fish soup — a warming and affordable option at around 1,800–2,200 ISK.

day_by_day.notes: The Herring Era Museum may have reduced winter hours — call ahead or check online. Stock up on groceries at the Samkaup-Strax store in town as options are limited and eating out every meal will strain a budget.

day_by_day.morning: Day trip to Ólafsfjörður via the Héðinsfjörður tunnel (about 20 minutes drive). Explore this equally charming small fishing village. Walk along the harbour and admire the mountain scenery surrounding the town — the peaks here are particularly dramatic in winter snow.
day_by_day.afternoon: Drive back through the tunnel and continue to Dalvík, a slightly larger town about 45 minutes from Siglufjörður. Visit the Hvoll Museum which includes a quirky exhibit about the tallest man in Iceland. Walk along the Dalvík waterfront and enjoy views across Eyjafjörður toward Akureyri.
day_by_day.evening: Return to Siglufjörður before dark. Spend the evening watching for Northern Lights from the hotel or a dark spot along the fjord. If skies are clear, this is one of the best possible locations in Iceland for aurora viewing due to minimal light pollution.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered — skyr with granola, coffee, and toast at the hotel.
meals.lunch: Grab a hot dog (pylsa) from a petrol station in Dalvík — Iceland's iconic budget snack at around 500–700 ISK each.
meals.dinner: Self-catered dinner at the hotel — pasta with canned fish or a simple stew using ingredients from the local store. Budget around 1,000–1,500 ISK for ingredients.

day_by_day.notes: Fuel up the car in Dalvík or Ólafsfjörður as petrol stations in Siglufjörður may have limited hours. Always check road.is for tunnel and road conditions before driving in January.

day_by_day.morning: Drive to Akureyri — Iceland's second largest city, about 1 hour from Siglufjörður via Dalvík and Route 82/1. Arrive and explore the compact city centre. Visit the iconic Akureyrarkirkja church perched on the hill above town — free entry and stunning architecture with beautiful stained glass windows.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore Akureyri's main shopping street, Hafnarstræti, and browse the local shops. Visit the Akureyri Art Museum (Listasafnið á Akureyri) for a budget-friendly cultural experience — entry around 1,500 ISK. Walk along the waterfront and enjoy views of Eyjafjörður, Iceland's longest fjord.
day_by_day.evening: Visit the Akureyri Swimming Pool (Sundlaug Akureyrar) — a fantastic budget activity at around 1,000–1,200 ISK entry. The outdoor hot pots are perfect for soaking while watching for Northern Lights on a clear evening. Return to Siglufjörður after your swim.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered at the hotel before departure.
meals.lunch: Akureyri has a Bonus supermarket — pick up supplies and eat a packed lunch, or try Bautinn restaurant for affordable traditional Icelandic food (soup of the day around 1,800 ISK).
meals.dinner: Strikið restaurant in Akureyri offers a good value lunch menu that sometimes extends to early evening, or try Greifinn for affordable pizza and pasta before the drive back. Budget 2,500–3,500 ISK.

day_by_day.notes: Akureyri is the main hub for the north — stock up on groceries at Bonus (Iceland's cheapest supermarket chain) to save significantly on food costs for the coming days. The drive back to Siglufjörður in the dark requires care on icy roads.

day_by_day.morning: Drive the Diamond Circle route — start with Goðafoss waterfall, about 45 minutes east of Akureyri on Route 1. This spectacular waterfall is one of Iceland's most beautiful and is free to visit. The name means 'Waterfall of the Gods' — in 1000 AD, a chieftain threw his Norse god statues into it after Iceland adopted Christianity.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue to Lake Mývatn, about 1 hour from Goðafoss. Visit the Námaskarð geothermal area (Hverir) — a surreal landscape of bubbling mud pots, steaming fumaroles and sulphur deposits. Completely free to visit and utterly otherworldly. Also explore the Mývatn lava fields (Dimmuborgir) — free walking trails through dramatic lava formations.
day_by_day.evening: Visit the Mývatn Nature Baths (Jarðböðin við Mývatn) — a more affordable alternative to the Blue Lagoon at around 5,500 ISK entry. Soak in the geothermal lagoon surrounded by volcanic landscape. Then drive back to Siglufjörður (about 1.5 hours). Watch for Northern Lights on the return journey.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered early breakfast before the long day trip.
meals.lunch: Packed lunch eaten at Goðafoss or Mývatn — bring a thermos of hot soup or coffee from the hotel.
meals.dinner: Gamli Bærinn café near Mývatn for a warming bowl of lamb soup before the drive back, or self-cater on return. Budget 1,800–2,500 ISK if eating out.

day_by_day.notes: This is a long day — approximately 200km of driving round trip. Start early to make the most of the limited daylight hours. The Mývatn Nature Baths are significantly cheaper than the Blue Lagoon and equally beautiful. Dress in waterproof layers for the geothermal areas as steam and spray are constant.

day_by_day.morning: Rest morning in Siglufjörður — sleep in and recover from the previous day's long drive. Take a slow walk along the harbour in the morning light (sunrise around 11:00 in January). Visit the small local swimming pool in Siglufjörður — a community geothermal pool at very low cost (around 800–1,000 ISK) and a great way to meet locals.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore the Siglufjörður valley on foot — walk up the road toward the old avalanche barriers above town. The mountains surrounding the fjord are prone to avalanches in winter, and the protective structures are an interesting feature of the landscape. Views from the valley road are spectacular.
day_by_day.evening: Northern Lights photography session — set up near the harbour or on the hillside above town. The reflection of the aurora in the fjord waters can be spectacular. Even without a camera, simply lying back and watching the lights dance is a magical free experience.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered — eggs, toast, and coffee at the hotel.
meals.lunch: Kaffi Rauðka for their daily soup special — warming and affordable at around 1,500–1,800 ISK.
meals.dinner: Self-catered — cook a hearty lamb stew or fish dish using ingredients from the local store. Icelandic lamb is excellent quality and reasonably priced from supermarkets.

day_by_day.notes: January is avalanche season in Siglufjörður — the town has been hit by devastating avalanches historically. Do not venture off marked paths on the hillsides above town. The local swimming pool is a wonderful budget activity and a genuine slice of Icelandic daily life.

day_by_day.morning: Drive the Tröllaskagi Peninsula — head south from Siglufjörður along Route 76 toward Hofsós. The coastal road offers dramatic views of the fjords and mountains. Stop at viewpoints along the way to photograph the winter landscape. The drive to Hofsós takes about 45 minutes.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit Hofsós — a tiny, picturesque village with one of Iceland's most beautifully situated swimming pools, the Hofsós Swimming Pool, perched on a cliff above the fjord with panoramic views. Entry around 800–1,000 ISK. Soak in the outdoor hot pots while gazing across Skagafjörður. Also visit the Icelandic Emigration Centre (Vesturfarasetrið) if open — it tells the story of Icelanders who emigrated to North America.
day_by_day.evening: Drive back to Siglufjörður via Sauðárkrókur — the largest town in the Skagafjörður region. Stop for supplies at the local supermarket. Return to Siglufjörður for the evening. Northern Lights watch from the hotel.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered at the hotel.
meals.lunch: Packed lunch eaten at Hofsós with views of the fjord.
meals.dinner: Self-catered dinner at the hotel using supermarket supplies from Sauðárkrókur — better selection and prices than the Siglufjörður convenience store.

day_by_day.notes: The Hofsós pool is one of Iceland's hidden gems and far less crowded than the famous Blue Lagoon. The Tröllaskagi Peninsula road can be icy and narrow in January — drive carefully and check road.is before departure. The Icelandic Emigration Centre may have limited winter hours.

day_by_day.morning: Drive to Varmahlíð in Skagafjörður valley — about 1 hour from Siglufjörður. Visit the Glaumbær turf farm museum, one of Iceland's best-preserved historic turf farmhouses. Entry around 2,000 ISK. The traditional turf buildings date back centuries and give a fascinating insight into how Icelanders survived the harsh winters historically.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore the Skagafjörður valley — drive to Víðimýrarkirkja, a beautifully preserved 19th-century turf church (free to view from outside). Continue to the Skagafjörður Heritage Museum for more regional history. The valley is known for its horse breeding — you may spot Icelandic horses in the fields.
day_by_day.evening: Return to Siglufjörður via the scenic Route 75 along the eastern shore of Skagafjörður. Stop at a viewpoint to watch for Northern Lights over the fjord on the drive back. The open landscape of the valley offers excellent aurora viewing conditions.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered early breakfast before departure.
meals.lunch: Café at Glaumbær (Áss café) — known for traditional Icelandic pancakes (pönnukökur) with cream and jam, a delicious and affordable treat at around 1,200–1,500 ISK.
meals.dinner: Self-catered at the hotel — simple pasta or rice dish with canned fish or vegetables.

day_by_day.notes: Glaumbær is one of Iceland's most important cultural heritage sites and well worth the entry fee. The Skagafjörður region is famous for Icelandic horse breeding and the annual horse round-up (réttir) — though that happens in autumn, you may still see horses in the fields in winter.

day_by_day.morning: Full rest and relaxation day in Siglufjörður. Sleep in, enjoy a slow breakfast, and spend the morning reading or relaxing at the hotel. The short winter days make this a natural pace for a budget trip — conserve energy and money with a quieter day.
day_by_day.afternoon: Walk the full length of the Siglufjörður fjord road — head north from town along the fjord shore as far as the road goes. The scenery is dramatic with steep mountains plunging into the dark fjord waters. Look for seabirds along the shoreline. This is a completely free activity.
day_by_day.evening: Visit the Siglufjörður swimming pool for an evening soak — the outdoor hot pots are particularly magical on a clear night when Northern Lights may be visible overhead. Then enjoy a cosy evening at the hotel with a good book.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered — a proper cooked breakfast using hotel facilities: eggs, toast, skyr, and coffee.
meals.lunch: Self-catered — rye bread with smoked lamb (hangikjöt) or smoked salmon, a classic Icelandic combination.
meals.dinner: Treat yourself to dinner at Kaffi Rauðka — try the fish of the day or lamb soup. Budget around 2,500–3,500 ISK as a mid-trip treat.

day_by_day.notes: Rest days are important on a budget trip — they save money and allow you to recharge. January weather can be unpredictable and sometimes a day of storms makes outdoor activities impossible anyway. Use this day to plan the second half of the trip and check weather forecasts.

day_by_day.morning: Drive to Akureyri again for a different experience — visit the Akureyri Botanical Garden (Lystigarðurinn), the world's most northerly botanical garden. Free entry. Even in January the garden has a stark, beautiful quality with snow-covered paths and dormant plants. Then visit the Nonni House museum — childhood home of beloved Icelandic author Jón Sveinsson.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore the Kjarnaskógur forest just south of Akureyri — Iceland's most visited forest and a popular local recreation area. Walking trails wind through the birch trees. In winter it has a magical, quiet atmosphere. Free to visit. Then browse the Akureyri flea market (Glerártorg shopping centre area) for budget souvenirs.
day_by_day.evening: Visit the Akureyri Swimming Pool again for a longer soak, or attend a local event if anything is happening in town. Drive back to Siglufjörður watching for Northern Lights on the return journey through the dark fjord landscape.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered before departure.
meals.lunch: Bonus supermarket in Akureyri — stock up on supplies and eat a packed lunch in the botanical garden or forest.
meals.dinner: Self-catered using fresh supplies from Bonus — cook a proper meal at the hotel. Icelandic lamb chops from Bonus are excellent value and quality.

day_by_day.notes: Use the Akureyri Bonus visit to stock up on supplies for the remaining days of the trip — this will significantly reduce food costs. The Kjarnaskógur forest is a lovely free activity that most tourists miss entirely.

day_by_day.morning: Drive to Húsavík — about 1.5 hours from Siglufjörður via Akureyri and Route 85. Húsavík is Iceland's whale watching capital, though whale watching tours don't operate in January. Instead, visit the Húsavík Whale Museum (Hvalasafnið) — an excellent museum with full whale skeletons and exhibits. Entry around 2,200 ISK.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore Húsavík town — walk along the harbour, visit the beautiful Húsavíkurkirkja church (free), and enjoy the views across Skjálfandi Bay. On clear days you can see across to the mountains of the Tjörnes peninsula. Drive to the Tjörnes peninsula for dramatic coastal views and fossil-rich cliffs.
day_by_day.evening: Drive back toward Siglufjörður — stop at Goðafoss waterfall again if time permits, as it looks completely different in the late afternoon winter light. The waterfall is illuminated by the last light of day in a spectacular way. Return to Siglufjörður for the evening.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered early breakfast before the long drive.
meals.lunch: Gamli Baukur restaurant in Húsavík — a historic harbour-side restaurant known for fish soup and seafood. Budget around 2,000–2,500 ISK for soup and bread.
meals.dinner: Self-catered at the hotel — use supplies from previous Bonus shop.

day_by_day.notes: Húsavík is a long day trip from Siglufjörður — approximately 300km round trip. Consider whether the drive is worthwhile given fuel costs on a tight budget. An alternative is to spend the day exploring closer areas around Siglufjörður and Tröllaskagi more deeply.

day_by_day.morning: Final full day — spend the morning doing anything you haven't yet done in Siglufjörður. Revisit favourite spots, take final photographs of the harbour and mountains, and pick up any last souvenirs from the local shop. The Herring Era Museum gift shop has affordable local crafts and books.
day_by_day.afternoon: Drive to the end of the Siglufjörður valley road for a final hike — walk as far as conditions safely allow toward the head of the fjord. The valley narrows dramatically and the mountain scenery is at its most impressive here. This is a completely free and memorable way to spend a final afternoon.
day_by_day.evening: Final Northern Lights hunt — this is your last chance for aurora viewing. Head to the darkest spot you can safely reach near Siglufjörður. Check the aurora forecast carefully and if conditions are good (clear skies, KP index 3+), stay out as long as possible. Celebrate the trip with a final dinner out.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered — use up remaining hotel food supplies.
meals.lunch: Kaffi Rauðka for a final lunch in Siglufjörður — try anything you haven't yet eaten from their menu.
meals.dinner: Splurge slightly on a final dinner at Kaffi Rauðka or the hotel restaurant — try traditional Icelandic lamb or Arctic char. Budget 3,000–4,500 ISK as a farewell treat.

day_by_day.notes: Pack bags tonight ready for an early departure tomorrow. Check the aurora forecast one final time — January 27th could be your best chance if previous nights were cloudy. Leave nothing behind at the hotel and confirm any transport arrangements for the journey to the airport tomorrow.

day_by_day.morning: Check out of Hotel Siglunes and begin the journey south to Keflavik International Airport. The drive is approximately 4.5–5 hours. Depart Siglufjörður early to allow plenty of time. Drive south via Akureyri and then Route 1 (the Ring Road) through the interior highlands toward Reykjavik.
day_by_day.afternoon: Stop at Borgarnes or Mosfellsbær for a final Icelandic meal before reaching the airport. If time permits, make a brief stop at the Deildartunguhver hot spring near Borgarnes — Europe's most powerful hot spring, free to view from the roadside. Arrive at Keflavik Airport with plenty of time before departure.
day_by_day.evening: Depart Iceland with memories of Northern Lights, hot springs, dramatic fjords, and the unique magic of the Icelandic winter. The remote north of Iceland around Siglufjörður offers an authentic, crowd-free experience that most tourists never see.

meals.breakfast: Early self-catered breakfast at the hotel before checkout — use up any remaining food supplies.
meals.lunch: N1 petrol station stop on Route 1 — Icelandic petrol stations serve surprisingly good and affordable hot food including lamb soup, sandwiches and the famous pylsur (hot dogs). Budget 1,500–2,000 ISK.
meals.dinner: Airport meal at Keflavik — budget around 2,500–3,500 ISK for a final meal, or bring snacks from the road to save money.

day_by_day.notes: Allow extra time for the drive in January — road conditions can be challenging and Route 1 through the highlands can be icy or subject to closures. Always check road.is before departing. Fill up the rental car with petrol before returning it to avoid expensive airport fuel surcharges. The Flybus from BSI terminal to the airport costs around 3,500 ISK if not driving.

day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Keflavik International Airport at 06:10. Clear customs and collect luggage. Pick up pre-booked rental car (4WD essential for winter Iceland travel). Drive to Reykjavik city center (~45 min) for a warm breakfast before beginning the long drive north to Siglufjörður.
day_by_day.afternoon: Begin the scenic drive from Reykjavik to Siglufjörður (~5–6 hours, approx 390 km via Route 1 and Tunnel 76). Stop at Borgarnes for a stretch and fuel. Continue through the Westfjords-adjacent highlands. Pass through Akureyri area and head into the dramatic fjord roads leading to Siglufjörður. Check in to Hotel Siglunes upon arrival.
day_by_day.evening: Settle into Hotel Siglunes. Take a short walk along the quiet harbor of Siglufjörður to get oriented. Enjoy a relaxed dinner at the hotel or a nearby local restaurant. Keep an eye on the northern lights forecast — Siglufjörður's remote location and minimal light pollution make it an excellent aurora-watching spot. Step outside after dinner to scan the skies.

meals.breakfast: Café at Keflavik Airport or a bakery in Reykjavik such as Brauð & Co — grab a skyr, pastry, and coffee (~1,500–2,000 ISK)
meals.lunch: Packed snacks or a quick stop at a petrol station diner along Route 1 in Borgarnes (~1,000–1,500 ISK)
meals.dinner: Siglufjörður Restaurant or Hotel Siglunes dining room — try local lamb soup or pan-fried Arctic char (~3,500–5,000 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Day 1 is primarily a travel day. Do not schedule strenuous activities — rest is essential after an overnight flight. Download the Veður app (Icelandic Met Office) and the Aurora Forecast app before leaving the airport. Ensure the rental car has winter tires and check road conditions at road.is before driving. The tunnel into Siglufjörður (Héðinsfjarðargöng) is single-lane in sections — drive carefully.

day_by_day.morning: After a good night's rest, enjoy a leisurely hotel breakfast. Take a morning walk through Siglufjörður town — explore the charming colorful harbor buildings, the old herring factory area, and the snow-dusted mountain backdrop. Visit the Herring Era Museum (Síldarminjasafnið), one of Iceland's best regional museums, which tells the story of the town's booming herring industry (~1,500 ISK entry).
day_by_day.afternoon: Drive to the nearby Hofsós Swimming Pool (~45 min south on Route 76), one of Iceland's most scenic geothermal pools perched on a cliff overlooking Skagafjörður fjord. Swim in the naturally heated outdoor pool with stunning winter fjord views. Return to Siglufjörður in the late afternoon and warm up with hot chocolate at a local café.
day_by_day.evening: Northern lights watch from the Siglufjörður harbor or the hillside above town. The town's isolation and dark skies make this one of the best aurora-viewing locations in Iceland. Dress in full thermal layers. If the forecast is strong (KP index 3+), drive a few kilometers out of town on Route 76 for even darker skies.

meals.breakfast: Hotel Siglunes breakfast buffet — skyr, eggs, smoked salmon, rye bread (~included or ~2,000 ISK)
meals.lunch: Café Rauðka in Siglufjörður — homemade soup and bread, a local favorite (~2,000–2,500 ISK)
meals.dinner: Hannes Boy Restaurant in Siglufjörður — cozy atmosphere, fresh fish dishes and Icelandic lamb (~4,000–5,500 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Hofsós Pool is open year-round but hours may be limited in winter — call ahead or check online. Bring a swimsuit, towel, and flip-flops. The drive on Route 76 is scenic but can be icy — drive slowly and check road.is. January aurora activity is statistically high due to long dark nights.

day_by_day.morning: Drive to Akureyri (~1.5 hours south via Route 82 and Route 1), Iceland's second-largest city and the 'Capital of the North.' Explore the charming downtown area — stroll along Hafnarstræti, visit the iconic Akureyrarkirkja church perched on the hill, and browse local shops. Stop at Brynja ice cream parlor, a beloved local institution open year-round.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit the Akureyri Botanical Garden (Lystigarðurinn) — even in winter the grounds are beautiful under snow. Then head to the Akureyri Swimming Pool (Sundlaug Akureyrar), a large geothermal facility with multiple hot tubs, steam rooms, and a waterslide — a perfect mid-trip warm-up. Spend 1.5–2 hours relaxing in the thermal waters.
day_by_day.evening: Enjoy dinner in Akureyri before driving back to Siglufjörður. Alternatively, if aurora forecast is excellent, park on the outskirts of Akureyri or pull over on Route 82 on the return drive for aurora viewing over the fjord.

meals.breakfast: Hotel Siglunes breakfast before departure
meals.lunch: Strikið Restaurant in Akureyri — panoramic views, fresh fish and burger options (~2,500–3,500 ISK)
meals.dinner: Rub23 in Akureyri — popular mid-range sushi and Icelandic fusion restaurant (~4,500–6,000 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Akureyri is a great resupply point — stock up on groceries, medications, or gear at Nettó or Krónan supermarket. The drive back to Siglufjörður in the dark requires extra caution on icy mountain roads. Check road.is before departing Akureyri.

day_by_day.morning: Explore the Tröllaskagi Peninsula (Trolls' Peninsula) — drive south from Siglufjörður along Route 76 through dramatic mountain scenery. Stop at Hofsós village for views over Skagafjörður. Continue to Sauðárkrókur, the largest town in Skagafjörður, and visit the local swimming pool and hot pots for a morning soak.
day_by_day.afternoon: Drive to the Glaumbær Turf Farm Museum (~30 min from Sauðárkrókur) — a beautifully preserved 18th-century turf farmstead that offers a fascinating glimpse into traditional Icelandic rural life (~1,800 ISK entry). Explore the interconnected turf buildings and the adjacent Áshús wooden house. Return to Siglufjörður via the scenic coastal route.
day_by_day.evening: Quiet evening in Siglufjörður. Visit the town's geothermal hot pot (outdoor public hot tub near the harbor) for a free or low-cost soak. Northern lights watch from the harbor — bring a thermos of hot tea. If skies are clear, this is one of the best evenings for aurora photography given the fjord reflection possibilities.

meals.breakfast: Hotel Siglunes breakfast
meals.lunch: Kaffi Krókur in Sauðárkrókur — homemade Icelandic food, lamb and fish dishes (~2,000–3,000 ISK)
meals.dinner: Self-catered dinner at hotel using groceries from Akureyri — Icelandic lamb chops, skyr dessert (~1,500–2,000 ISK per person)

day_by_day.notes: Glaumbær may have reduced winter hours — verify opening times before visiting. The Tröllaskagi Peninsula roads can be challenging in winter; check conditions. The public hot pot in Siglufjörður is a wonderful local experience — ask hotel staff for the exact location.

day_by_day.morning: Day trip to Húsavík, the 'Whale Watching Capital of Iceland' (~2 hours east via Route 1 and Route 85). In winter, whale watching tours are limited, but the town itself is charming. Visit the Húsavík Whale Museum (Hvalasafnið) for an excellent introduction to North Atlantic whale species (~2,200 ISK). Walk along the colorful harbor.
day_by_day.afternoon: Drive to the Mývatn region (~45 min from Húsavík) — one of Iceland's most geologically active and visually stunning areas. Visit the Námaskarð geothermal area (Hverir) — a surreal landscape of bubbling mud pots, steaming fumaroles, and sulfurous vents. Then explore the Dimmuborgir lava field, a maze of dramatic lava formations with easy walking paths.
day_by_day.evening: Soak at the Mývatn Nature Baths (Jarðböðin við Mývatn) — a less-crowded alternative to the Blue Lagoon with similar milky-blue geothermal waters set against a volcanic landscape (~5,500 ISK). Enjoy the hot tubs and steam cave as darkness falls. Drive back to Siglufjörður (~2.5 hours) — check aurora forecast before departing.

meals.breakfast: Hotel Siglunes breakfast before early departure
meals.lunch: Gamli Baukur in Húsavík — iconic harbor-side restaurant, fish soup and fresh catch (~2,500–3,500 ISK)
meals.dinner: Mývatn Nature Baths café for a light meal, or pack sandwiches for the drive back (~1,000–2,000 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: This is a long day (~5–6 hours of driving total) — start early. Mývatn Nature Baths are open until 22:00, making an evening soak perfectly timed. The sulfur smell at Námaskarð is strong but harmless. Bring a camera with a wide-angle lens for aurora photography on the return drive.

day_by_day.morning: Rest morning in Siglufjörður — sleep in and enjoy a slow breakfast. Take a snowshoe walk or winter hike on the lower slopes above town (ask hotel for recommended safe winter routes). The mountains surrounding Siglufjörður are dramatic and beautiful under snow. Alternatively, visit the Herring Era Museum again for any exhibits missed on Day 2.
day_by_day.afternoon: Drive to Ólafsfjörður (~20 min south through the tunnel) — a small, picturesque fishing village. Walk around the harbor and explore the quiet streets. Visit the local swimming pool with hot tubs for an afternoon soak (~900 ISK). Return to Siglufjörður and spend time in the hotel relaxing, reading, or planning the upcoming southern Iceland leg of the trip.
day_by_day.evening: Dedicated northern lights hunting evening. Drive 10–15 km out of Siglufjörður on Route 76 toward Hofsós for maximum darkness. Bring a tripod, camera, warm sleeping bag to sit on, and hot drinks. Stay out for 2–3 hours monitoring the sky. If aurora appears, this location offers stunning reflections over the fjord.

meals.breakfast: Hotel Siglunes breakfast — leisurely pace
meals.lunch: Café Rauðka in Siglufjörður — soup of the day and fresh bread (~2,000 ISK)
meals.dinner: Hannes Boy Restaurant — try the catch of the day or Icelandic lamb with root vegetables (~4,000–5,500 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Day 6 is intentionally lighter to prevent travel fatigue. Use the afternoon to do laundry if needed (ask hotel). Check the 3-day aurora forecast — if tonight looks poor, save the dedicated aurora hunt for a better night. Dress in extreme cold-weather layers for the evening watch: base layer, mid layer, windproof outer shell, hat, gloves, and insulated boots.

day_by_day.morning: Begin the drive south from Siglufjörður toward Reykjavik (~5 hours). Stop at Blönduós on Route 1 for a coffee break. Continue through the vast Icelandic interior highlands (Route 1 stays coastal in winter — the interior F-roads are closed). Enjoy the dramatic winter landscape of lava fields, snow-covered mountains, and frozen rivers.
day_by_day.afternoon: Stop at Hraunfossar and Barnafoss waterfalls near Borgarnes (~2 hours from Reykjavik) — a series of springs emerging from a lava field directly into the Hvítá river, creating a magical curtain of water. Even in winter these are spectacular and rarely crowded. Continue to Reykjavik and check into a mid-range guesthouse or hotel for 2 nights (pre-booked).
day_by_day.evening: Explore Reykjavik's Laugavegur street — browse shops, galleries, and warm up in a café. Visit Hallgrímskirkja church exterior for the iconic view. Enjoy dinner in the city center. Check aurora forecast — if strong, take a taxi or Uber to the Grótta lighthouse on the Seltjarnarnes peninsula (~15 min from center) for city-edge aurora viewing.

meals.breakfast: Hotel Siglunes final breakfast before checkout
meals.lunch: Petrol station or roadside café stop along Route 1 — lamb soup or hot dog (~1,000–1,500 ISK)
meals.dinner: Messinn Restaurant in Reykjavik — excellent mid-range seafood, famous for their pan-fried fish (~4,500–6,000 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Book Reykjavik accommodation in advance — January is quieter but good places fill up. Return the northern rental car if switching to a city-based vehicle, or keep the 4WD for the remaining days. The Icelandic hot dog (pylsa) from Bæjarins Beztu Pylsur stand is a must-try Reykjavik experience (~500 ISK).

day_by_day.morning: Blue Lagoon Geothermal Spa experience (~45 min from Reykjavik near Keflavik). Book the Comfort package in advance (~12,000–15,000 ISK) — includes silica mud mask, algae mask, and drink. Arrive at opening time (08:00) to beat crowds. Soak in the iconic milky-blue 38–40°C geothermal waters surrounded by black lava fields. Enjoy the in-water bar and steam rooms.
day_by_day.afternoon: Return to Reykjavik by early afternoon. Visit the National Museum of Iceland (Þjóðminjasafn Íslands) on Suðurgata — excellent exhibits on Viking settlement, medieval Iceland, and modern history (~2,000 ISK). Walk through the old Reykjavik harbor area (Grandi) and visit the Whales of Iceland exhibition if interested (~3,500 ISK).
day_by_day.evening: Northern Lights Hunting Tour — join a guided evening tour departing from Reykjavik (~9,000–12,000 ISK). Expert guides use real-time aurora forecasts and cloud cover data to drive to the best viewing locations outside the city. Tours typically run 3–4 hours and include aurora photography tips. Most tours offer a free rebooking if aurora doesn't appear.

meals.breakfast: Early breakfast at Reykjavik hotel before Blue Lagoon departure — or grab a pastry at a bakery
meals.lunch: Blue Lagoon LAVA Restaurant — mid-range option inside the lagoon complex, Icelandic fish and lamb dishes (~3,500–5,000 ISK)
meals.dinner: Grillmarkaðurinn (The Grill Market) in Reykjavik — Icelandic ingredients cooked over lava stone grill, mid-range splurge (~5,500–7,500 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Blue Lagoon MUST be pre-booked online — walk-ins are not accepted. Book at least 2–3 weeks in advance for January. Bring a hair tie as the silica can tangle long hair. The Northern Lights tour is weather-dependent — book with a company offering free rebooking (e.g., Arctic Adventures, Reykjavik Excursions, or Guide to Iceland).

day_by_day.morning: Golden Circle day trip from Reykjavik (~3–4 hours of driving total). Start at Þingvellir National Park — walk the Almannagjá rift valley between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates, visit the historic Alþingi parliament site, and see the crystal-clear Silfra fissure (snorkeling/diving experience — see afternoon). The park is stunning under winter snow.
day_by_day.afternoon: Snorkeling in Silfra Fissure at Þingvellir — join a guided snorkel tour between the tectonic plates in 2–4°C glacially filtered water with visibility up to 100 meters (~19,000–22,000 ISK including dry suit). This is a once-in-a-lifetime experience. After the tour, continue the Golden Circle: visit the Geysir geothermal area (see Strokkur erupt every 5–10 minutes) and Gullfoss waterfall.
day_by_day.evening: Return to Reykjavik. Warm up with a hot shower and dinner. Visit the Reykjavik City Library or a cozy bar on Laugavegur. If energy allows, check aurora forecast for a late-night walk to Grótta lighthouse.

meals.breakfast: Reykjavik hotel breakfast or Sandholt Bakery on Laugavegur — excellent pastries and coffee (~2,000 ISK)
meals.lunch: Geysir Center café or packed lunch — soup and sandwich (~2,000–2,500 ISK)
meals.dinner: Sægreifinn (The Sea Baron) in Reykjavik harbor — famous lobster soup and grilled fish skewers, excellent value (~3,000–4,000 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Silfra snorkeling requires advance booking and a medical waiver. Minimum age is typically 12. The dry suit keeps you dry but the water is extremely cold — fingers and face will feel the chill. Bring warm clothes to change into immediately after. Gullfoss and Geysir are free to visit. Þingvellir National Park has a small parking fee (~750 ISK).

day_by_day.morning: Drive the South Coast from Reykjavik toward Vík (~2.5 hours). Stop at Seljalandsfoss waterfall — in winter the path behind the falls may be icy/closed, but the exterior view is spectacular. Continue to Skógafoss waterfall — climb the 527 steps to the top for panoramic views over the snow-covered coastal plain. The frozen spray creates incredible ice formations in January.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue to Reynisfjara Black Sand Beach near Vík — one of the world's most dramatic beaches with towering basalt columns (Reynisdrangar sea stacks), powerful Atlantic waves, and jet-black volcanic sand. Exercise extreme caution — sneaker waves are deadly year-round. Photograph the beach from a safe distance. Drive into Vík village and explore the iconic Vík í Mýrdal church on the hill.
day_by_day.evening: Drive back toward Reykjavik or stay overnight in Vík/Selfoss area (pre-booked guesthouse) to position for Day 11's glacier hike. Enjoy a quiet dinner. Check aurora forecast — the South Coast has excellent dark skies and the black sand beach with aurora overhead is a legendary photography opportunity.

meals.breakfast: Reykjavik hotel breakfast before early departure
meals.lunch: Skógarfoss Café near the waterfall — lamb soup and sandwiches (~2,000–2,500 ISK)
meals.dinner: Suður-Vík Restaurant in Vík — cozy local restaurant, fish and chips or lamb stew (~3,500–4,500 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Reynisfjara Beach is genuinely dangerous — never turn your back on the ocean and stay well above the wave line. The waves can reach 10–15 meters with no warning. Seljalandsfoss path behind the falls is typically closed in winter due to ice — do not attempt if roped off. If staying overnight near Vík, book accommodation in advance.

day_by_day.morning: Drive to Skaftafell in Vatnajökull National Park (~1.5 hours east of Vík). Meet your guide for the Skaftafell Glacier Hike on Vatnajökull — strap on crampons and hike across Europe's largest glacier with a certified glacier guide (~12,000–15,000 ISK for a 3-hour tour). Explore stunning blue ice formations, crevasses, and moulins. The glacier landscape in winter is otherworldly.
day_by_day.afternoon: After the glacier hike, visit the nearby Svartifoss waterfall in Skaftafell — a short 1.5 km hike through birch forest to a dramatic waterfall framed by hexagonal basalt columns. Then drive to the Jökulsárlón Glacier Lagoon (~45 min east) — watch enormous blue icebergs calve from the Breiðamerkurjökull glacier and float in the lagoon. Walk to Diamond Beach where ice chunks wash ashore on black sand.
day_by_day.evening: Begin the drive back west toward Reykjavik (~4.5 hours). Stop for dinner in Kirkjubæjarklaustur ('Klaustur') — a small village with a good restaurant. Check aurora forecast on the drive — the South Coast is one of the best aurora corridors in Iceland. Pull over safely if aurora appears.

meals.breakfast: Guesthouse breakfast near Vík or packed breakfast from supermarket
meals.lunch: Skaftafell Visitor Center café — soup, sandwiches, and hot drinks (~2,000 ISK)
meals.dinner: Systrakaffi in Kirkjubæjarklaustur — homemade Icelandic food, lamb and fish (~3,500–4,500 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Glacier hiking requires sturdy waterproof hiking boots (crampons provided by tour operator). Wear warm, waterproof layers. Book the glacier hike well in advance — January tours fill up. Jökulsárlón is free to visit and open year-round. The drive back to Reykjavik is long — consider an overnight stop in Selfoss if tired (~1 hour from Reykjavik).

day_by_day.morning: Return to Reykjavik. Visit the Secret Lagoon Natural Hot Spring in Flúðir (~1.5 hours from Reykjavik via Route 35) — Iceland's oldest swimming pool (1891), a naturally heated geothermal pool surrounded by bubbling hot springs and a small geyser that erupts every few minutes (~3,000 ISK). Far less crowded than the Blue Lagoon with a more authentic, rustic atmosphere. Soak for 1.5–2 hours.
day_by_day.afternoon: Return to Reykjavik. Spend the afternoon exploring the city properly — visit the Reykjavik Art Museum (Kjarvalsstaðir branch, ~1,800 ISK), walk through the Tjörnin lake area (often partially frozen in January with birds), and explore the colorful streets of the old town. Visit the Harpa Concert Hall on the harbor for its stunning geometric glass facade.
day_by_day.evening: Final dedicated Northern Lights Hunting Tour or self-guided aurora watch. If the previous tour on Day 8 was clouded out, rebook tonight. Alternatively, drive to Þingvellir National Park independently (~45 min from Reykjavik) for dark-sky aurora viewing — the park is free to enter at night. Celebrate the trip with a special dinner.

meals.breakfast: Reykjavik hotel breakfast or Brauð & Co bakery
meals.lunch: Flúðir village café near Secret Lagoon — light lunch, soup and bread (~2,000 ISK)
meals.dinner: Fiskmarkaðurinn (The Fish Market) in Reykjavik — upscale Icelandic-Asian fusion, a memorable final dinner (~6,000–8,500 ISK per person)

day_by_day.notes: Secret Lagoon must be pre-booked online. The lagoon is small and intimate — maximum 50 people at a time. Bring a towel and swimsuit. The small geyser near the pool erupts approximately every 5 minutes — a delightful bonus. Tonight is the last realistic aurora opportunity — prioritize it if skies are clear.

day_by_day.morning: Final morning in Iceland. Enjoy a leisurely hotel breakfast. Pack and check out. Take a final walk along Reykjavik's harbor waterfront — visit the Sun Voyager (Sólfar) sculpture for a last iconic Iceland photo. Browse the Kolaportið flea market if it's open (weekends only — check schedule) or pick up last-minute souvenirs on Laugavegur: Icelandic wool lopapeysa sweaters, skyr, lava salt, and local chocolate.
day_by_day.afternoon: Drive to Keflavik International Airport (~45 min from Reykjavik). Return the rental car at the airport — allow 30–45 minutes for the return process. Check in for your departure flight. Enjoy a final Icelandic meal at the airport.
day_by_day.evening: Departure from Keflavik International Airport. Reflect on 13 incredible days of northern lights, geothermal hot springs, glaciers, waterfalls, and the raw beauty of Iceland in winter.

meals.breakfast: Hotel breakfast — final Icelandic spread with skyr, smoked salmon, and rye bread
meals.lunch: Reykjavik café or airport restaurant — fish soup or lamb sandwich (~2,500–3,500 ISK)
meals.dinner: Airport dining at Keflavik — Fiskfélagið or airport café (~3,000–4,000 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Return the rental car with a full tank of fuel — petrol stations near the airport include N1 and Orkan. Allow extra time at the airport for security (Keflavik can be busy even in January). Duty-free at Keflavik is excellent for Icelandic spirits (Brennivín), chocolate, and cosmetics. Keep one layer of warm clothing accessible in your carry-on for the flight. Total estimated mid-range budget for 13 days (excluding flights and accommodation): approximately 250,000–350,000 ISK (~$1,800–$2,500 USD) per person.

highlights: Mix of paid and free experiences

trip_options.title: Premium Iceland Escape
trip_options.description: Indulge in the best the destination has to offer. Premium flights, luxury hotels, and exclusive experiences.

experiences.name: Northern Lights Hunting Tour
experiences.description: Join a guided evening tour away from Reykjavik's light pollution to witness the aurora borealis dancing across the sky. Expert guides use real-time forecasts to find the best viewing spots, and you'll learn about the science behind this natural phenomenon while capturing stunning photographs.

experiences.name: Blue Lagoon Geothermal Spa
experiences.description: Soak in the world-famous milky-blue geothermal waters rich in silica and minerals. Enjoy in-water massages, silica mud masks, and swim-up bars while surrounded by dramatic lava fields. Book the Comfort package for access to the main lagoon, towel rental, and one silica mud mask.

experiences.name: Snorkeling or Diving in Silfra Fissure
experiences.description: Snorkel or dive between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates in crystal-clear glacial water with visibility up to 100 meters. The surreal blue and green hues of the water make this one of the most unique natural experiences on Earth, guided by certified instructors.

experiences.name: Secret Lagoon Natural Hot Spring
experiences.description: Relax in Iceland's oldest swimming pool, a naturally heated geothermal pool surrounded by bubbling hot springs and a small geyser that erupts every few minutes. Far less crowded than the Blue Lagoon, this authentic experience offers a peaceful soak amid stunning Icelandic countryside.

experiences.name: Skaftafell Glacier Hike on Vatnajökull
experiences.description: Strap on crampons and hike across Europe's largest glacier with an expert guide. Explore stunning ice formations, deep blue crevasses, and ash layers from ancient volcanic eruptions. The hike offers breathtaking panoramic views of the surrounding black sand plains and mountain peaks.

day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Keflavík International Airport at 06:10. Clear customs and collect luggage. Transfer via pre-arranged luxury private car service northward toward Siglufjörður — a scenic 4.5–5 hour drive through the Snæfellsnes Peninsula and Tröllaskagi mountain peninsula. Rest and enjoy the dramatic winter landscapes en route.
day_by_day.afternoon: Arrive in Siglufjörður early afternoon. Check in to Hotel Siglunes on Lækjargata 10. Freshen up and settle into your premium room overlooking the fjord. Take a gentle self-guided stroll through the charming, snow-dusted herring capital town — explore the colorful harbor, the old fish factory district, and the quiet streets framed by steep mountain walls.
day_by_day.evening: Wrap up warm and step outside or onto the hotel terrace for your first Northern Lights watch from Siglufjörður — the town's minimal light pollution and fjord-framing mountains create an exceptional aurora corridor. Keep the Aurora Forecast app handy (aim for KP index 3+).

meals.breakfast: Light refreshments at the airport lounge or packed provisions from the private transfer service.
meals.lunch: Stop en route at Hótel Búðir or a quality roadside café in Borgarnes for a warm bowl of Icelandic lamb soup and fresh-baked rye bread.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Hotel Siglunes's own restaurant — indulge in pan-seared Arctic char with dill butter, roasted root vegetables, and a glass of crisp Icelandic craft beer or Scandinavian white wine.

day_by_day.notes: Pre-arrange your private airport transfer well in advance. The drive is long but spectacular — pack a neck pillow and a thermos of coffee. January daylight in Siglufjörður is very limited (roughly 5–6 hours), so the afternoon stroll should begin immediately after check-in. Dress in full thermal layers for the evening aurora watch.

day_by_day.morning: After a leisurely breakfast, visit the award-winning Herring Era Museum (Síldarminjasafnið) — one of Iceland's finest regional museums, housed across three restored harbor buildings. Explore the fascinating story of the 20th-century herring boom that built Siglufjörður, complete with authentic boats, equipment, and period interiors.
day_by_day.afternoon: Drive or arrange a guided 4WD excursion into the Tröllaskagi Peninsula hinterland. Explore the dramatic mountain passes and frozen valleys around Siglufjörður, including views over Héðinsfjörður — an abandoned fjord accessible via a short tunnel. Stop at scenic overlooks for photography of the snow-covered peaks and frozen fjord surfaces.
day_by_day.evening: Return to town for a relaxing soak at the Siglufjörður community geothermal swimming pool (Sundlaug Siglufjarðar) — a local hot pot experience with mountain views, far more intimate than the tourist-heavy south. Follow with a Northern Lights vigil from the harbor pier.

meals.breakfast: Full Icelandic breakfast at Hotel Siglunes — skyr with berries, smoked lamb, rye bread, soft-boiled eggs, and strong coffee.
meals.lunch: Warm lunch at Kaffi Rauðka, Siglufjörður's beloved local café — try the fish soup and homemade cinnamon buns.
meals.dinner: Back at Hotel Siglunes — slow-braised Icelandic lamb shank with juniper jus, mashed root vegetables, and a curated Scandinavian red wine pairing.

day_by_day.notes: The Herring Era Museum may have limited winter hours — confirm opening times the evening before. The mountain road toward Héðinsfjörður can be icy; use a 4WD vehicle and check road conditions at road.is before departing. The community pool is a genuine local experience — bring a towel and flip-flops.

day_by_day.morning: Depart Siglufjörður early and drive south along Route 76 and then Route 1 (Ring Road) toward Akureyri — Iceland's 'Capital of the North,' approximately 1.5 hours away. Arrive and explore the charming town center: visit the iconic Akureyrarkirkja church perched above the city, stroll the pedestrian Hafnarstræti shopping street, and browse the Akureyri Art Museum.
day_by_day.afternoon: Drive approximately 45 minutes east of Akureyri to the Mývatn region — one of Iceland's most geothermally active and visually stunning areas. Visit the Námaskarð geothermal field (Hverir) — a surreal landscape of bubbling mud pots, steaming fumaroles, and sulfurous vents set against rust-red rhyolite mountains. Then explore the bizarre Dimmuborgir lava formations — a labyrinth of volcanic pillars and arches.
day_by_day.evening: Soak in the Mývatn Nature Baths (Jarðböðin við Mývatn) — a premium geothermal lagoon with milky-blue mineral-rich waters set against a volcanic landscape, far less crowded than the Blue Lagoon. Enjoy the outdoor hot tubs and steam baths as darkness falls and aurora potential rises.

meals.breakfast: Early breakfast at Hotel Siglunes before departure.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Rub23 in Akureyri — one of the north's finest restaurants, known for premium sushi and Icelandic seafood with Asian-fusion influences.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Vogafjós Farm Restaurant near Mývatn — a unique farm-to-table experience where you can watch cows being milked through a glass wall while dining on smoked trout, geothermal rye bread baked underground, and farm-fresh dairy desserts.

day_by_day.notes: Check road conditions on Route 1 east of Akureyri — this stretch can be challenging in January. The Mývatn Nature Baths are open until 22:00, making them ideal for combining with aurora watching. Book the Mývatn Nature Baths in advance. Consider staying overnight near Mývatn if road conditions are poor — Hótel Laxá is an excellent luxury option nearby.

day_by_day.morning: Morning exploration of the Mývatn area (if staying overnight) or return drive from Siglufjörður. Visit Goðafoss — the 'Waterfall of the Gods' — one of Iceland's most dramatic and historically significant waterfalls, where the chieftain Þorgeir threw his Norse idols into the water upon Iceland's conversion to Christianity in 1000 AD. The winter ice formations around the falls are spectacular.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue to the Skútustaðagígar pseudo-craters on the southern shore of Lake Mývatn — walk the circular trail around these unique volcanic formations created when lava flowed over wetlands. Then visit Grjótagjá cave — a small lava cave with a crystal-clear geothermal pool (viewing only; swimming is restricted). Return to Siglufjörður via Akureyri (approximately 2.5 hours total).
day_by_day.evening: Quiet evening at Hotel Siglunes. Enjoy a premium in-room spa treatment if available, or relax in the hotel lounge with Icelandic schnapps (Brennivín) and local cheeses. Step outside periodically for aurora monitoring.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at Vogafjós Farm Restaurant or Hótel Laxá if staying overnight near Mývatn, or at Hotel Siglunes.
meals.lunch: Packed premium lunch box arranged by Hotel Siglunes, or stop at Bautinn Restaurant in Akureyri — a classic Icelandic grill known for generous portions of lamb and fish.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Hotel Siglunes — pan-fried cod with langoustine bisque, crispy capers, and seasonal Icelandic vegetables, paired with a crisp Chablis.

day_by_day.notes: Goðafoss is accessible year-round and particularly magical in winter with ice formations — wear crampons or ice cleats on the viewing paths. The Grjótagjá cave featured in Game of Thrones and is a popular photo stop. Confirm return road conditions before departing Mývatn.

day_by_day.morning: Full rest and recovery morning at Hotel Siglunes. Sleep in, enjoy a long leisurely breakfast, and spend time reading or journaling in the hotel lounge with fjord views. This is a deliberate slow day to recharge mid-trip.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore the Siglufjörður valley on a guided snowshoe or winter hiking excursion into the mountains directly above the town. The steep fjord walls offer incredible views over the harbor and surrounding peaks. A local guide can be arranged through the hotel — routes vary by snow conditions and fitness level.
day_by_day.evening: Dedicated Northern Lights Hunting Tour — arrange a private guided aurora excursion from Siglufjörður. A local expert will drive you to optimal dark-sky locations in the surrounding fjords and mountain passes, away from any ambient light. Bring a tripod for long-exposure photography.

meals.breakfast: Extended breakfast at Hotel Siglunes — full spread with smoked salmon, Icelandic cheeses, fresh pastries, and specialty coffee.
meals.lunch: Light lunch at Kaffi Rauðka — homemade soup, open-faced sandwiches, and hot chocolate.
meals.dinner: Special premium dinner at Hotel Siglunes — request the chef's tasting menu if available, featuring a curated progression of Icelandic ingredients: langoustine, reindeer, skyr panna cotta, and local berry compote.

day_by_day.notes: The snowshoe excursion should be booked through the hotel concierge at least one day in advance. January is statistically one of the best months for Northern Lights in Iceland — clear nights in Siglufjörður, away from Reykjavik's glow, offer exceptional aurora probability. Download the Vedur.is app for real-time cloud cover forecasts.

day_by_day.morning: Drive west along the scenic Tröllaskagi coastal road (Route 76) to the village of Hofsós — approximately 1 hour from Siglufjörður. Visit the Hofsós Emigration Center, which tells the story of Icelandic emigration to North America in the 19th century. Then soak in the extraordinary Hofsós Infinity Pool — a geothermal swimming pool perched on a cliff edge with panoramic views over Skagafjörður fjord and the mountains beyond.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue south to Sauðárkrókur — the largest town in Skagafjörður. Visit the Skagafjörður Heritage Museum (Byggðasafn Skagfirðinga) to learn about the region's Viking-age history and horse culture. Skagafjörður is Iceland's horse heartland — if time permits, arrange a short Icelandic horse experience at a local farm.
day_by_day.evening: Return to Siglufjörður via the mountain tunnel. Enjoy a quiet evening with a premium whisky tasting at the hotel bar — ask the staff to curate a selection of Icelandic and Nordic spirits alongside imported single malts.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at Hotel Siglunes before departure.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Kaffi Krókur in Sauðárkrókur — a cozy local café with excellent fish dishes and homemade cakes.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Hotel Siglunes — grilled Icelandic lamb chops with rosemary and garlic, roasted potatoes, and a robust Argentinian Malbec.

day_by_day.notes: The Hofsós Infinity Pool is one of Iceland's most photogenic geothermal pools — arrive early to avoid any crowds. Bring a waterproof camera or phone case for pool photography. The Icelandic horse experience should be pre-booked; farms in Skagafjörður include Hestur og Maður and Lýtingsstaðir.

day_by_day.morning: Drive south from Siglufjörður toward the Snæfellsnes Peninsula — approximately 3.5–4 hours. En route, stop at Glaumbær turf farm museum near Varmahlíð — a beautifully preserved 18th-century turf farmstead that offers a vivid window into traditional Icelandic rural life.
day_by_day.afternoon: Arrive on the Snæfellsnes Peninsula and explore Snæfellsjökull National Park. Visit the dramatic Djúpalónssandur black pebble beach with its sea stacks and shipwreck remnants. Then drive to Arnarstapi and walk the coastal cliffside trail to Hellnar — a stunning 2.5 km path past basalt columns, sea arches, and nesting seabirds (even in winter, the geology is extraordinary).
day_by_day.evening: Check in to a premium guesthouse or hotel on the Snæfellsnes Peninsula (e.g., Hótel Búðir — one of Iceland's most romantic and atmospheric hotels, set beside a black lava field and a historic white church). Enjoy the remote, dark-sky location for aurora watching.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at Hotel Siglunes before departure.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Hótel Hamar near Borgarnes — excellent panoramic views over Borgarfjörður and a solid menu of Icelandic classics.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Hótel Búðir's acclaimed restaurant — one of Iceland's finest dining experiences outside Reykjavik, featuring locally sourced lamb, langoustine, and seasonal ingredients with an exceptional wine list.

day_by_day.notes: This is a travel-heavy day — depart Siglufjörður by 08:00 to make the most of the limited daylight. Hótel Búðir should be booked well in advance as it is small and highly sought after. The Djúpalónssandur beach has lifting stones (Dvergasteinar) — try your hand at the traditional strength test.

day_by_day.morning: Full exploration of Snæfellsjökull National Park. Drive to the Snæfellsjökull glacier — the mystical ice-capped volcano immortalized by Jules Verne as the entrance to the Earth's core in 'Journey to the Center of the Earth.' Take a guided snowcat or snowmobile tour onto the glacier summit for panoramic views across the peninsula and, on clear days, all the way to Reykjavik.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit Vatnshellir lava tube cave — a guided tour descending 35 meters into an 8,000-year-old lava tube with dramatic geological formations. Then explore the Lóndrangar basalt sea stacks and the Malarrif lighthouse area — iconic Snæfellsnes coastal scenery.
day_by_day.evening: Return to Hótel Búðir for a relaxing evening. Enjoy the hotel's hot tub under the open sky, watching for the Northern Lights over the black lava fields. The Búðir area is one of Iceland's premier dark-sky locations.

meals.breakfast: Full breakfast at Hótel Búðir — fresh pastries, Icelandic dairy, smoked fish, and premium coffee.
meals.lunch: Packed premium lunch on the glacier or at the Snæfellsjökull visitor center café.
meals.dinner: Second evening at Hótel Búðir restaurant — try the slow-cooked lamb neck with root vegetable purée and a Burgundy Pinot Noir, followed by skyr cheesecake with crowberry coulis.

day_by_day.notes: The glacier snowcat tour must be pre-booked through Snjófell or a similar operator — January conditions can be extreme on the summit, so dress in full expedition-grade outerwear. The Vatnshellir cave tour runs year-round but has limited winter slots — book in advance. Check road conditions around the peninsula tip (Route 574) as it can be icy.

day_by_day.morning: Depart Snæfellsnes and drive south toward the Reykjanes Peninsula — approximately 2.5 hours. Stop at the Deildartunguhver hot spring near Reykholt — Europe's most powerful hot spring, pumping 180 liters of near-boiling water per second from the earth. Visit the nearby Krauma Geothermal Baths — a premium, design-forward spa fed directly by Deildartunguhver, with five geothermal pools, a cold pool, and a relaxation room.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue to the Reykjanes Peninsula and check in to a luxury hotel near the Blue Lagoon (e.g., Silica Hotel — the exclusive boutique hotel directly adjacent to the Blue Lagoon with private lagoon access). Spend the afternoon at the world-famous Blue Lagoon Geothermal Spa — enjoy the milky-blue silica-rich waters, in-water massages, the premium Lava Restaurant, and the exclusive Retreat Spa if booked.
day_by_day.evening: Linger at the Blue Lagoon into the evening — the lagoon is open until 22:00 and is magical after dark, with steam rising against the night sky and aurora potential overhead. Enjoy a glass of Icelandic sparkling water or champagne at the in-water bar.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at Hótel Búðir before departure.
meals.lunch: Light lunch at Krauma Geothermal Baths café — soup, sandwiches, and herbal teas.
meals.dinner: Dinner at the Blue Lagoon's Lava Restaurant — a premium dining experience built into a lava cave, featuring Icelandic seafood, lamb, and an extensive wine cellar. Reserve well in advance.

day_by_day.notes: Book the Blue Lagoon and Silica Hotel well in advance — January is still popular and premium slots fill quickly. The Retreat Spa at the Blue Lagoon is an ultra-luxury add-on (private lagoon, in-water treatment rooms) — worth the splurge for a luxury trip. Krauma Baths near Reykholt are a hidden gem and far less crowded than the Blue Lagoon.

day_by_day.morning: Drive to Þingvellir National Park — approximately 45 minutes from the Reykjanes Peninsula. Explore the UNESCO World Heritage Site where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates meet and where Iceland's ancient parliament (Alþingi) was founded in 930 AD. Walk the Almannagjá rift valley and Öxará river gorge — dramatic even under winter snow.
day_by_day.afternoon: Snorkeling or Diving in Silfra Fissure — join a guided premium dry-suit snorkel or dive tour between the tectonic plates in Silfra, part of Þingvellir National Park. The water is a constant 2–4°C but crystal-clear with visibility up to 100 meters — one of the world's top dive sites. Dry suits are provided; no prior diving experience needed for snorkeling.
day_by_day.evening: Drive to Reykjavik (approximately 45 minutes) and check in to a luxury city hotel (e.g., The Retreat at Blue Lagoon, or Hótel Borg — Reykjavik's iconic art deco landmark). Explore the city's vibrant evening scene: visit the Harpa Concert Hall, stroll Laugavegur, and enjoy Iceland's famous nightlife.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at Silica Hotel before departure.
meals.lunch: Packed warm lunch provided by the Silfra tour operator — essential after the cold water experience.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Dill Restaurant in Reykjavik — Iceland's first Michelin-starred restaurant, offering a Nordic tasting menu that celebrates Icelandic ingredients with extraordinary creativity. Book months in advance.

day_by_day.notes: The Silfra snorkel/dive requires advance booking through DIVE.IS or Arctic Adventures — dry suit experience is recommended but not mandatory for snorkeling. You must not fly within 18–24 hours of diving (relevant for the return flight). Þingvellir is magical in winter — the frozen lake and snow-covered rift valley are breathtaking. Wear waterproof boots.

day_by_day.morning: Explore Reykjavik's cultural highlights: visit Hallgrímskirkja church and take the elevator to the tower for panoramic city views. Walk to the Perlan museum — a stunning glass-domed building with an immersive Northern Lights planetarium show, a real ice cave, and exhibits on Icelandic nature and geology.
day_by_day.afternoon: Drive the Golden Circle route: visit Geysir geothermal area — home to the original Geysir and the reliably erupting Strokkur (every 5–10 minutes). Continue to Gullfoss waterfall — Iceland's most iconic waterfall, partially frozen in January with dramatic ice formations. End at Þingvellir for a second, more leisurely exploration if desired.
day_by_day.evening: Return to Reykjavik. Join a premium Northern Lights Hunting Tour departing from the city — a guided minibus tour to optimal dark-sky locations outside Reykjavik, with expert aurora forecasting and photography guidance. Tours typically run 21:00–01:00.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at your Reykjavik luxury hotel — full buffet spread.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Friðheimar tomato farm restaurant near Geysir — a unique greenhouse restaurant serving tomato-based dishes grown on-site using geothermal energy. Book in advance.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Grillið Restaurant at Radisson Blu Saga Hotel — Reykjavik's rooftop fine dining destination with panoramic city views, featuring premium Icelandic lamb, seafood, and an award-winning wine list.

day_by_day.notes: Friðheimar is a must-visit — the tomato soup and fresh bread are legendary. Book well in advance. The Golden Circle roads are generally well-maintained in winter but can be icy — a 4WD rental is recommended. The Northern Lights tour should be booked through a reputable operator such as Reykjavik Excursions or Arctic Adventures.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the Secret Lagoon Natural Hot Spring (Gamla Laugin) in Flúðir — approximately 1.5 hours from Reykjavik. Iceland's oldest swimming pool (established 1891) is a naturally heated geothermal pool surrounded by bubbling hot springs, steaming geysers, and a wooden boardwalk. Far more intimate and authentic than the Blue Lagoon, with a maximum of 50 guests at a time.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore the South Coast: drive east along Route 1 to visit Seljalandsfoss waterfall — walk behind the curtain of water (icy in January — crampons essential) — and Skógafoss waterfall, where ice formations create a magical winter spectacle. Continue to the black sand beach at Reynisfjara near Vík — dramatic basalt columns, sea stacks, and powerful Atlantic waves.
day_by_day.evening: Return to Reykjavik. Spend the final evening exploring the city's premium dining and bar scene. Visit Slippbarinn at Icelandair Hotel Reykjavik Marina for creative cocktails, or Kex Hostel bar for a more local atmosphere. End the night with a final aurora watch from Grótta lighthouse on the Seltjarnarnes peninsula — a short drive from the city center.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at your Reykjavik hotel.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Skál! in Reykjavik's Hlemmur Food Hall — a vibrant market hall with premium Icelandic street food, craft beer, and natural wines.
meals.dinner: Farewell dinner at Óx Restaurant — Reykjavik's most exclusive and intimate dining experience, a 12-seat counter restaurant with a single nightly tasting menu of extraordinary Icelandic ingredients. Reservations are extremely limited — book months ahead.

day_by_day.notes: The Secret Lagoon should be booked in advance online. Crampons or ice cleats are essential at Seljalandsfoss in January — the path behind the waterfall is extremely icy. Reynisfjara beach has dangerous sneaker waves — stay well back from the water's edge and heed all warning signs. Óx Restaurant is one of Iceland's hardest reservations — if unavailable, Matur og Drykkur is an excellent alternative celebrating traditional Icelandic recipes.

day_by_day.morning: Final morning in Reykjavik. Enjoy a long, leisurely breakfast at the hotel. Visit the National Museum of Iceland (Þjóðminjasafn Íslands) for a comprehensive overview of Icelandic history from the Settlement Age to the present — a fitting cultural conclusion to the trip. Browse the museum gift shop for premium Icelandic souvenirs: lopapeysa wool sweaters, handcrafted jewelry, and artisan food products.
day_by_day.afternoon: Last-minute shopping on Laugavegur and Skólavörðustígur streets — pick up Icelandic design items, Geysir wool goods, Omnom chocolate, and Brennivín spirits. Visit the Kolaportið flea market (open weekends) for local crafts and vintage finds. Transfer to Keflavík International Airport — allow at least 2.5 hours before departure, including the 45-minute drive.
day_by_day.evening: Departure from Keflavík International Airport. Relax in the premium lounge before boarding. Reflect on 13 extraordinary days of Northern Lights, geothermal wonders, volcanic landscapes, and world-class Icelandic hospitality.

meals.breakfast: Final full Icelandic breakfast at the hotel — make it count.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Messinn Restaurant in Reykjavik — celebrated for its cast-iron pan-fried fish dishes, a perfect final taste of Iceland's seafood heritage.
meals.dinner: Dinner at the airport or on the flight — or enjoy a final snack at the Keflavík airport's premium lounge.

day_by_day.notes: Confirm your departure flight time and work backward to ensure you arrive at Keflavík with ample time — the airport is 45–50 minutes from central Reykjavik. Return your rental car at the airport. Pack any geothermal spa products (silica mud, mineral salts) in checked luggage if over 100ml. Iceland's duty-free at Keflavík is excellent — stock up on Icelandic spirits, chocolate, and skincare on the way out.
